Analyse this alien creature description and extract the 10 Ward biological feature dimensions.

CREATURE DESCRIPTION:
The creature is called a **veil-skimmer**, a slow, cold-blooded animal of an ammonia ocean. It is built for a world where the seas stay liquid only far below water’s freezing point, where chemistry runs on nitrogen rather than the familiar water-based toolkit, and where “wet” means something sharp, thin, and bitterly cold.

### Setting
Its ocean is liquid ammonia, roughly −70 to −40 °C, under a dense nitrogen–hydrogen atmosphere streaked with methane haze. Sunlight is weak and amber. The sea is less viscous than water and evaporates more readily, so waves are quick and fine, and shore ice of frozen ammonia and water-ice crusts the shallows. Dissolved salts, metal amides, and simple nitriles drift in the solvent the way ions and organics do in Earth’s seas.

### Body
An adult is about two meters long and flat, like a manta crossed with a lily pad. Its body is a flexible lattice of nitrogen-rich polymers—chains closer to polyamides and nitrile-linked scaffolds than to Earth proteins—held in a gel that does not freeze solid at these temperatures. The “skin” is not a lipid bilayer of the water-world kind. Those membranes would dissolve or fail here. Instead it wears a woven sheath of fluorocarbon-like and long-chain nitrile sheets, beaded with charged ammonium groups that keep the interior chemistry partitioned from the sea.

Color is dull bronze and soot-black, tuned to absorb the little red light that reaches the surface and to shed heat slowly. Along the margins run translucent fringes, almost like kelp blades. They are not leaves. They are heat exchangers and chemical gills: thin sheets that let small molecules cross while the charged sheath holds larger solutes inside.

It has no bones. Internal pressure and a cartilage-like mesh of cross-linked amides keep its shape. Six radial “ribs” of stiffer polymer let it camber the body like a wing, so it can glide just under the surface or sink into slower, denser layers.

### Metabolism
Energy does not come from breathing oxygen. Oxygen is scarce and, at these temperatures, a poor partner for its chemistry. The veil-skimmer runs on redox gradients already present in the ammonia sea: it oxidizes dissolved hydrogen and simple hydrocarbons against nitrogen-bearing oxidants—nitriles, hydrazine-like intermediates, metal amides leached from the crust. The reactions are slow. Its tissues are built for that. A meal of hydrocarbon slick and mineral-rich silt can last for weeks.

“Blood” is a circulating ammonia-amide solution carrying complexed metals—iron and nickel centers caged in nitrogen ligands—that shuttle electrons. There is no hemoglobin-red. Cut it, and the fluid is pale straw, smelling, if you could smell it without freezing, faintly of amines.

Waste nitrogen is not a burden the way urea is for us. Nitrogen is the solvent’s own element. It vents surplus hydrogen and light organics through the fringe-gills and keeps a tight internal pool of ammonium and amide ions, the acid–base pair that replaces water’s hydronium and hydroxide.

### Senses and movement
Eyes are useless in the haze below a few meters, so the eyes are small and only for the surface: two low domes that track the bright smear of the sun and the glitter of floating hydrocarbon films. Most of its world is felt chemically. The fringes are dense with receptors that taste amides, metal ions, and the faint ammonia-soluble “scent” of other veil-skimmers—long, stable nitrile markers that linger for days in the cold.

It hears by pressure. A line of fluid-filled sacs along the ribs picks up the tick of distant ice calving and the thump of larger animals turning in the deep. Movement is a slow undulation. Bursts are rare; speed costs heat and solvent, and both are expensive. When threatened it folds, dumps a cloud of bitter metal-amide mucus that fouls a predator’s chemical sense, and sinks.

### Life cycle
Reproduction is external and patient. Two adults trail complementary strands of genetic polymer—information stored not in DNA as we know it, but in a repeating nitrogenous backbone stable in ammonia—into a quiet eddy. The strands pair in the solvent itself, then accrete a gel coat. Embryos drift as clear beads for years, photosynthesizing weakly with pigments that catch red and near-infrared, and scavenging dissolved organics. Most never meet a parent.

Adults gather where upwelling brings metal-rich fluid and where methane rain from the haze dissolves into the sea. They are not social in any loud way. They share currents, and sometimes a feeding film, and recognize one another by those long chemical names written in nitriles.

### What it is not
It is not a fish in a different costume. Its solvent freezes water, boils near temperatures we call winter, dissolves many Earth fats, and runs acid–base chemistry on ammonium and amide instead of H₃O⁺ and OH⁻. The veil-skimmer’s slowness, its strange blood, its sheath instead of skin, and its years-long childhood are all consequences of that one fact: the ocean it calls home is ammonia, and everything alive in it has had to agree.

Outer layers are rich in long, nonpolar chains that do not dissolve in ammonia; inner layers hold charged nitrogen groups that let ions pass in a controlled way. In the cold, the membrane stays fluid because the molecules are branched and loosely packed, the way some Earth organisms use unsaturated lipids, but here the trick is structural rather than a familiar fat. Frost-like crystals of ammonium salts sometimes rim the trailing edges; the animal sheds them the way a lizard sheds skin.

It does not breathe oxygen. Its metabolism runs on redox chemistry available in an ammonia sea: reduced nitrogen compounds and metal ions from hydrothermal seeps, oxidized species drifting down from the upper ocean where ultraviolet light cracks ammonia and other gases. Along its flanks are rows of copper- and iron-centered reaction sites embedded in protein-like polymers. They glow faintly blue-green when the animal is working hard—chemiluminescence from the energy-harvesting reactions, visible in the black water like a string of dim lanterns.

The head is not a head in our sense. At the front is a broad, keeled plate of harder tissue, edged with chemoreceptive filaments. Ammonia carries dissolved scents extremely well; the filaments taste gradients of amines, metal ions, and the bitter trace of a seep miles away. There are no image-forming eyes. When it needs a burst—escaping a larger grazer, or closing on a drifting mat of polymer “snow”—it vents a pulse of dissolved gas through vents near the tail. Beneath the keel, a ventral groove lined with sticky, nitrogenous mucilage traps flakes of organic precipitate and microbial mats torn from vent chimneys. Cilia-like beating filaments, themselves ammonia-stable polymers, move the slurry into internal chambers where metal-centered catalysts break it down. Waste leaves as ammonium-rich brine and a faint trail of lighter organics. Other, smaller organisms follow that trail the way Earth fish follow a ship’s wake.

Those that do anchor, feed on the chemical gradient, and over many slow years lengthen into keel-singers.

“Singer” is not metaphor alone. When two adults pass in the dark, they modulate the stiffness of their lattices so that the pressure wave of their swimming carries a simple pattern: identity, size, whether they are ripe to release packets. The sound is a low, almost subsonic thrum, swallowed quickly by the cold sea. To anything with the right pits, the abyss is never quiet. It is a sparse choir of keels, each announcing that it is still here, still tasting the ammonia, still following the faint metallic breath of the world beneath the ice.
